newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY SAYS EMU MEMBERSHIP POSSIBLE BY 2005.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY SAYS EMU MEMBERSHIP POSSIBLE BY 2005.

text.p: Hungary is likely to be ready for European Union (EU) membership by around 2000 but its high inflation rate will probably not qualify it for European Monetary Union (EMU) before 2005, the Finance Ministry said.
"Hungary's economy will allow it to become a stable EU member by the turn of the millenium, or one or two years later," Deputy Secretary of State Tamas Tetenyi told a business conference on Friday.
"But according to calculations related to inflation, we cannot reach a position to meet the (EMU's) Maastricht criteria before 2005," he added.
Hungary is one of the several EU associate members in eastern Europe which are building a market economy and hope to reach fully-fledged EU membership by around 2000.

Tetenyi said Hungary took a large step towards the EU and the EMU in 1995 when it reached whjat he called an economic breakthrough as an austerity programme and a surge of privatisation revenues helped it reverse the rapid expansion of the state debt.

However, the state debt is still around 80 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), compared to an EMU requirement of a maximum 60 percent, and privatisation revenues will soon dry up as the sell-offs are completed in 1998, he said.
Tetenyi added that consequently Hungary's only way to reduce the state debt further is to speed up GDP growth.

If the growth rate increases to three percent in the short term and five percent by around 2000 from the current figure around one percent, and income policies remain firm, Hungary will be able to meet the Maastricht debt criterion within a few years, he said.

However, inflation, currently over 20 percent, is also well above the EMU requirements, and this will force Hungary to continue its preannounced crawling-peg devaluation policy for several years so as to preserve the competitiveness of Hungarian companies, Tetenyi said.
A country can only join the EMU if it has not devalued its currency for two years.

By around 2000, when Hungary is likely to join the EU, the country's forint will be ready to integrate into the European monetary system, though inflation will be still above that of other EU members, he said.
"The Hungarian currency has a small volume, so it will be relatively easy to hold it within the European monetary system on an intervention basis," he said.
Once it is in EU, Hungary, with the help of the Union, will probably reduce its inflation rate more easily than now, so as to meet EMU inflation and interest rate requirements, he added.
The inflation rate required for EMU membership is based on the average rate of the three countries in the EU with the lowest inflation and currently stabds at around three percent.
